title: A Saudi court sentenced a Kenyan mother to 100 lashes. She is still trying to bring her son home.
subtitle: Esther Wanja Muthoni had travel papers from the Kenyan embassy, but a criminal case kept her in Saudi Arabia until they expired. Kenya now says it is engaging Saudi authorities on her case.
author: ATHENA

paragraphs.text: Esther Wanja Muthoni had been trying for more than a year to take her son home to Kenya when a court in Riyadh sentenced her to 100 lashes and a year of banishment. On 11 November, Kenya’s foreign affairs principal secretary, Korir Sing’oei, said his government was engaging Saudi authorities. He did not announce a date for mother and child to come home.

Muthoni, 40, gave birth to her son in August 2025 in the staff accommodation where she lived as a domestic worker. A supervisor took them to hospital, where police questioned her. The distinction is important: the court convicted her in October 2026 of having sex outside marriage. Giving birth was how the relationship came to the authorities’ attention.

According to The New York Times, which interviewed Muthoni and reviewed court records, she told police that the boy’s father, an Egyptian man, had left Saudi Arabia. The judgment gave no indication that authorities had pursued him. Muthoni, meanwhile, appeared at several hearings before three judges. She said the court provided an interpreter but no lawyer.

After police released her, Muthoni was turned away from her accommodation and from a shelter. For a time she and her baby lived at a Riyadh petrol station where other migrant mothers had gathered. After the Times reported on her situation in 2025, the company through which she worked provided lodging, and the Kenyan embassy issued travel papers. The criminal case prevented her from using them.

Saudi Arabia announced restrictions on judicial flogging in 2020, but the change did not cover every offence. It curtailed judges’ discretion to impose lashes while leaving in place punishments considered fixed under their interpretation of Islamic law. The Riyadh panel applied that exception in Muthoni’s case. Because such judgments are not routinely published, her case cannot establish how often courts still order the punishment.

Muthoni did not appeal. She told the Times she believed accepting the ruling offered her the best chance of seeing her other children in Kenya again. Yet the year of banishment does not guarantee deportation to Kenya, and her travel papers have expired. The Saudi government did not respond to the newspaper’s request for comment.

For Muthoni and her one-year-old son, Kenya’s diplomatic intervention leaves two questions unanswered: whether Saudi authorities will set aside the corporal punishment, and whether the two governments will arrange for them to travel home together.
